analysis.one_liner: Repeals the rule requiring locally prevailing wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without ever receiving a vote, so federal construction workers keep the prevailing-wage pay floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally funded construction — buildings, roads, and other public works — to pay workers the locally prevailing wage. This bill would wipe out that requirement entirely and cancel any references to it in other laws. Supporters say it would cut the cost of federal construction; opponents say it would let contractors pay construction workers less on projects the public is funding. The bill never advanced past its initial referral to committee and received no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Contractors bidding on federally financed construction would gain, because they could pay market wages rather than the prevailing-wage floor, reducing their labor costs. Taxpayers could benefit indirectly if savings are passed into lower bids.

how_it_helps.text: It would eliminate the requirement that locally prevailing wages be paid on federally financed construction, which supporters say lowers the cost of public buildings and works.

It would also void any other law's reference to Davis-Bacon wage requirements, wiping out the prevailing-wage floor across federally assisted construction, with an effective date 30 days after enactment and no change to contracts already in existence.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects, who would lose the prevailing-wage guarantee and likely see lower pay on those jobs.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the prevailing-wage floor would cut pay for construction workers on federally funded projects, where Davis-Bacon wages often exceed local market rates.

Savings to taxpayers are uncertain: contractors set bids, and studies of prevailing-wage rules suggest lower labor standards can bring less-experienced crews and uneven work quality, offsetting some of the cost savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost to workers is concrete: federal construction jobs would pay less, and research on past prevailing-wage rules suggests lower wages can also mean less-experienced crews and uneven work quality. The benefit — cheaper federal construction — is real but uncertain and would flow largely to project budgets and contractors rather than to most taxpayers in any visible way. On balance, the bill shifts risk and cost onto workers while offering the public only a speculative savings.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died there.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 30, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
The committee took no further action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill never received a House vote or moved in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers keep the prevailing-wage floor on federal projects; contractors who would have gained from lower labor costs did not.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal construction workers keeping their pay floor

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on January 30, 2017.

for.name: 12 House cosponsors
for.role: House Republicans including Reps. Franks, Sanford, Harper, Amash, Hensarling, Duncan, and Jenkins

for.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never advanced past committee in a House controlled by the same party, so no vote split was ever recorded.

industries.note: Contractors bidding on federal projects could pay whatever the local market allows instead of the prevailing wage, lowering their labor costs. The benefit to taxpayers of cheaper bids is uncertain because savings depend on contractors passing them through.

Union and other construction workers lose the wage floor that guarantees locally prevailing pay on federal work, which often exceeds what non-union contractors would otherwise pay. This is the group the bill would directly cut.
